newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE-NZ ride offers flight with strings attache.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-NZ ride offers flight with strings attache.

text.p: A New Zealander has people queueing to lie on a piece of aluminium and hurtle through the sky at break-neck speeds, at times just 1.5 metres (five feet) from the ground.
Neil Harrap's "Fly by Wire" invention, the first adventure ride offering full pilot control of a high-speed tethered plane, is attracting interest from around the world.
The concept is simple -- imagine dangling a pen from a piece of string and swinging it around beneath a central point. Now imagine the pen controlling its own speed and direction.
The Fly by Wire pilot is strapped prone into a four-metre rocket-shaped aluminium capsule, suspended from a single point among overhead wires strung across a gully.
The plane is first lifted from the ground, then winched backwards up the slope until the pilot's feet are almost directly above her head.
Once sufficient blood has rushed to the brain to convince the pilot that plunging into space is a good idea, she grasps the throttle and the release lever simultaneously. The ride begins.
PILOTS EXPERIENCE FORCES OF THREE G

The plane, powered by a 24-horsepower rear engine, flies to a maximum height of 65 metres (200 feet) and within a teeth-gnashing 1.5 metres of the ground in places. It reaches speeds of 120 kmh (75 mph) an hour on full throttle.
During the NZ$129 (US$82) six-minute ride, the pilot's visceral fortitude is challenged both by weightlessness and maximum G-forces of three times gravity.

It is humanly impossible to hit anything, but the plane has a kill switch to stop the motor in case of uncontrollable panic. Harrap said only one person had used the switch since the operation began in May.
The Fly by Wire experience is about as close as most mortals will come to flying a fighter jet.
Within seconds of the initial plunge down the hillside the plane has swooped low across the launching pad and is rushing headlong towards rocks on the opposite wall of the gully.
In a last-minute reprieve the plane pulls up for a hairpin turn, is suspended for a split second in which each blade of grass below is visible, then dives once more into the valley.
Cautious pilots can navigate the gully in a wide circle but Harrap recommends high speed and tight turns to maintain height.

The ride is by no means over when the timer stops, killing the motor. The plane soars silently above the earth for several minutes, the Tasman Sea a hazy blue in the distance and the only sound that of a small stream below, before the pilot is brought back to earth with a gentle bump.
Harrap said the plane, designed by aeronautical engineer John ten Have, meets all engineering and safety standards. Its support cable has a seven tonne breaking strain.

At present there is only one in operation, near the coastal town of Paekakariki, 40 km (30 miles) north of Wellington. However, the patent and trademark have been registered in 21 countries and Harrap has big plans.
FOREIGN INVESTORS ENTHUSIASTIC
Harrap said he had been approached by several foreign companies and individuals wanting to buy the system, including theme park operators and hoteliers.
However, while he was open to cooperation with parties in other countries, he considers it would be foolish to sell.
"Right now it's as though your house is worth $200,000, but you know in 12 months it will be worth $500,000, so would you sell it? The answer, of course, is no," he told Reuters.
"It could be idea to do a public company, a share offer in New Zealand or overseas. It's hard to know which way to go at the moment."
Parties in the United States, Hong Kong, Indonesia and Australia had expressed their interest, and Harrap said a German group was very keen to acquire European rights.
"They're anxious to proceed to the point where they're doing the research and looking at sites already, even though we don't have an agreement," he said.
Harrap's immediate priority is to build another Fly by Wire in Queenstown, New Zealand's tourist capital, where he expects strong demand and the ability to charge more per ride.

"It's still in development, but when we do the next one we expect to achieve speeds of at least 250 km an hour (150 mph). That will make it the fastest adventure ride...ever built in the world," he said.
